rows.selection_reason: No experiments have been completed, so the first priority is to establish a clean, minimal baseline that calibrates the search space. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible configuration: it uses a linear, well-understood encoder (PCA), requires no image processing or fusion, and has no aggregation complexity. This experiment will (1) confirm the pipeline runs end-to-end, (2) quantify how much signal is available from RNA data alone, and (3) set a performance floor against which all image-only and multimodal configurations can be compared. Choosing the simplest RNA baseline first is the most budget-efficient use of the first experiment because it is fast to execute (no image encoder or fusion overhead), minimizes the risk of confounding from multiple design choices, and directly informs whether the image modality or multimodal fusion is necessary to achieve strong performance. Subsequent experiments can then systematically add image modality, upgrade encoders, or test multiprofile aggregation with a clear reference point.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA → 48.5% acc), which provides a weak baseline and leaves the most critical question for a multimodal study unanswered: does image data carry a stronger or complementary signal? Testing config_010 (image-only, single-profile, ResNet50) establishes the image modality's standalone performance under the same profile setting as config_001, giving us a clean unimodal comparison. This is essential before evaluating any multimodal fusion configuration, because without knowing each modality's ceiling we cannot attribute gains (or losses) to fusion versus to a stronger single modality. If image alone substantially outperforms RNA, it reshapes the entire search toward image-centric or fusion-weighted configurations; if it is comparable, it motivates testing whether multimodal combination adds value. Under a tight budget, this single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most fundamental design axis (modality contribution) and directly informs the next 2–3 experiments.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% acc, while config_010 (image_only, resnet50) is only 20.8%, confirming RNA is the dominant modality. The current best RNA encoder is a simple linear PCA (2000 dims). Uncertainty: We have no evidence yet about whether a powerful learned RNA encoder (scgpt, a pretrained single-cell transformer) can extract substantially more signal than PCA. This experiment (config_007: rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001, isolating the RNA encoder choice. If scgpt significantly outperforms PCA, it validates investing in learned encoders and justifies exploring them in multimodal settings. If it does not, it indicates the RNA signal is already well-captured by linear structure, redirecting effort toward profile settings or fusion. Under a limited budget, resolving this high-impact, high-uncertainty question before testing multiprofile aggregation or multimodal fusion avoids confounding multiple design changes in a single experiment.

Evidence: RNA is clearly the dominant modality (pca_n2000 singleprofile acc=0.485 vs image-only resnet50 acc=0.208), and among tested RNA encoders pca_n2000 outperforms scgpt. However, we have zero data on whether multiprofile aggregation improves over singleprofile—a fundamental design axis that governs a large fraction of the remaining search space. This experiment (config_002) directly tests that question by taking our best-performing configuration (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) and changing only the profile setting to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). It isolates the multiprofile effect while holding the encoder constant, giving a clean comparison to config_001. Choosing avgpool over transformer avoids introducing a second confounding variable; if avgpool already shows a gain, we can then test transformer in a follow-up. Under a tight budget, resolving whether multiprofile is worth pursuing at all is the highest-information next step, as it determines whether the many multiprofile and multimodal-multiprofile configurations are worth further exploration.

The strongest evidence so far is that multiprofile + avgpool with PCA (config_002, acc=0.591) substantially outperforms singleprofile PCA (config_001, acc=0.485), indicating that multi-profile aggregation is a critical design axis. The natural next question is whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further improve on avgpool within the same multiprofile+PCA setup. config_003 is a clean single-variable change (avgpool → transformer) from the best result, so any performance difference can be attributed to the aggregation method. This is the best use of the next budget slot because it either confirms avgpool sufficiency (freeing us to explore other dimensions like multimodal fusion or alternative encoders) or reveals a further gain that justifies committing to transformer-based aggregation in subsequent multimodal experiments. Testing multimodal fusion now would be premature given the very weak image-only signal (config_010, acc=0.208), and testing alternative RNA encoders in multiprofile is lower priority since PCA already dominates scgpt in singleprofile.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) at 0.591 acc, while image-only resnet50 is very weak (0.208 acc). The critical open question is whether combining the strong RNA signal with the weak image signal via multimodal fusion yields any benefit over the RNA-only baseline. This experiment (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly extends the best-performing RNA configuration by adding the image modality with the simplest fusion strategy. It tests whether the image carries any complementary information not captured by RNA alone. This is the highest-information next step because: (1) it answers the fundamental multimodal question before investing further in image-encoder or fusion-variant experiments, (2) it builds on the strongest validated RNA setup (pca_n2000 + multiprofile + avgpool), and (3) the result will decisively guide whether to pursue weighted fusion, better image encoders (ViT-L), or refocus entirely on RNA-encoder improvements. Under a limited budget, resolving the 'does multimodal help at all?' question before branching into 30+ multimodal variants is the most efficient use of the next experiment.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multi, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the best result so far (acc=0.619, F1=0.610), showing that adding a weak image modality (ResNet50 alone: 0.208) via concat fusion to the strong RNA multi-avgpool baseline (0.591) yields a modest but consistent gain. The fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted) is a fundamental design choice that governs how the two modalities interact, and it is currently untested. Question: Does learned weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation for combining the (dominant) RNA features with the (weak) image features? This is a clean single-variable A/B against config_018, changing only the fusion mechanism. Why best next: It directly exploits the strongest configuration while resolving a high-leverage uncertainty—if weighted fusion helps, it reshapes the optimal recipe for every subsequent multimodal experiment (ViT-L, scGPT, transformer aggregation); if it does not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect budget toward stronger image encoders or alternative RNA encoders. This maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best (config_019, multimodal/multiprofile/PCA/ResNet50/avgpool/weighted, acc=0.639) was built on the finding that avgpool outperformed transformer in the RNA-only multi-profile setting (0.591 vs 0.519). However, that comparison was made without an image modality present. Question: Does transformer aggregation, which can model higher-order interactions, provide a benefit in the multimodal setting where it must integrate both aggregated multi-profile RNA features and image features? This is a single-variable change from the current best (only aggregation differs), making the result directly attributable to the aggregation choice. Why this is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, confirming or refuting the transferability of the avgpool>transformer finding to the multimodal context reduces uncertainty about a core architectural decision that will affect all future multimodal experiments. If avgpool is confirmed, we can lock it in and pivot to testing image encoder quality (ViT-L) or RNA encoder alternatives; if transformer unexpectedly helps, it reveals an important cross-modal interaction effect and reshapes the search space.

Evidence: The current best is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639). We know multiprofile+avgpool+weighted is the validated best combination, and PCA outperforms SCGPT for RNA. However, image-only ResNet50 was very weak (acc=0.208), raising uncertainty about whether the image modality's modest contribution in the multimodal setting (0.639 vs 0.591 RNA-only) is limited by encoder quality. Question: Does a stronger, more expressive image encoder (ImageNet ViT-L) provide substantially better complementary features that push multimodal performance higher? This experiment (config_025) is a clean single-variable swap from the current best—only the image encoder changes—so any performance shift is attributable to encoder quality. Why best next: It directly exploits the validated best pipeline while resolving the key uncertainty about the image modality's ceiling. A positive result opens a strong exploitation path; a null result tells us the image signal is inherently limited, redirecting budget toward RNA-side improvements (e.g., scvi_n200). Either outcome is highly informative under a limited budget.

The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, and scgpt was clearly inferior to PCA in single-profile RNA-only (0.411 vs 0.485). However, scvi_n200 has never been tested in any experiment, making the RNA encoder choice the largest remaining source of uncertainty in the best-performing configuration. config_031 tests scvi_n200 within the exact best-performing framework (multimodal, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted), isolating the encoder variable. If scvi_n200 matches or exceeds PCA, it opens a new optimization direction; if it underperforms, we can confidently rule it out and focus remaining budget on other levers (e.g., image encoder or profile count). This is the highest-information-gain experiment because it resolves a completely unexplored design axis while keeping all other settings at their empirically validated optima.
